The Oaks came up twice too, and in ways that don't quite match. Talia Finch went to West Oakland and found Elio Perez and Daniel Cloak and Darius Clark all saying, with genuine warmth, that the team is reaching toward the community and that it matters. Then Simon Leary spent his week with the A's record — 127-35, a machine more than a team by now — and asked the harder question: at what point does the architecture become the story, rather than the people passing through? Martin Richards, a veteran who knows something about being moved across positions and cities, told Simon that value shifts sometimes overnight. Ollie Campbell, who doesn't even follow sports closely, noticed people talking about how the A's keep winning no matter who's holding the beams. The Oaks engagement Talia documented and the A's apparatus Simon examined are two different models of what a sports franchise can be in this city. One is still trying to be recognized by its neighborhood. The other has achieved something so structural it barely needs anyone's recognition.

Outside, the A’s were winning again. They always were. 127-35, another number in a season of numbers. What does it mean when a machine—and make no mistake, that’s what this is now, not a team but an apparatus—keeps running no matter which gears are swapped out? How does a structure like that bear its own weight? Richards, who has no answers because no one does, only the numbers, squinted at the light through the blinds. “It’s not just about adapting—it’s about understanding that your value shifts, sometimes overnight.”

The A's, of course, broke through the fog in the way only playoff baseball can. Anthony Raines put us in the visiting clubhouse in New York where John Ellis sat with a towel over his shoulders after nine innings, four hits, zero earned runs, nine strikeouts. The A's closed the ALDS with a 4-0 win, and Ellis was not modest about what it meant: "We're here to win, and that performance was a statement." Eric Taveras, whose fourth-inning home run was the offensive signature of the night, told Raines that when your pitcher brings that kind of fire, the rest of the roster has no choice but to match it. Back in Fruitvale, Rick Walker and Rafael Pilgrim heard it on the radio and said the same thing independently — this team might have the pitching depth to go somewhere real. The question Raines left open is whether Ellis was a harbinger or an outlier. The ALCS will answer it, and I expect that answer to reverberate through every neighborhood in this city.

Taveras’ home run, his second of the series, was a solo shot in the fourth inning, part of a night where he went one-for-four with one RBI. It wasn’t a barrage of offense, but it didn’t need to be. Ellis’ performance rendered every run a luxury, not a necessity. Back in Oakland, the buzz was palpable. Rick Walker, tuning in from Fruitvale, caught the game on the radio. "I heard about John Ellis' shutout on the radio this morning—what a performance!" he said. "It’s got me thinking the A’s might just have the pitching depth to make a serious playoff run this year." Rafael Pilgrim echoed the sentiment: "I heard about John Ellis' shutout—nine innings, no runs. It’s got people here in Fruitvale buzzing, thinking the A’s might just have the pitching depth to go deep in the playoffs."

The next day, I met up with Travis Coles, the A's starting pitcher, at a coffee shop in Downtown. "I've felt the city's energy shift with our recent wins," Travis said, his eyes lighting up with excitement. "It's like the whole community is coming together and feeding off our momentum. As a player, it's an incredible feeling to know that our performance is having a direct impact on the people around us." As I walked out of the coffee shop, I ran into Clark Saryan, the Closing Pitcher for the Las Vegas Aviators. "I've seen how a win like that can bring the community together," Clark said, smiling. "It's like a spark that ignites a sense of pride and belonging. As someone who's been around the game, I know how it feels to be part of a team that's on a roll, and I think that energy is infectious. It's not just about the game itself, but about the way it makes people feel - like they're part of something bigger than themselves."

Dr. Lila Mezran's reporting this cycle gave us Yu Zen listening from a hospital bed in Rockridge to nurses talking about neighborhood impacts — "It's not just numbers, it's families, neighbors." What the reporting doesn't yet answer — and what I want answered — is whether the concentration of illness in Chinatown and East Oakland reflects something structural about care access in high-density neighborhoods, or whether this is seasonal pressure landing where it always lands. That question isn't rhetorical. I'm asking Jordan Velez to look at it from the business side next cycle, because the Temescal picture he drew this week — the tight-knit rhythm of Gridiron Analytics and OakTown Social and Temescal Community Health Center all nodding to each other across three blocks — suggests that neighborhood economic health and community health are not separate ledgers. Trevor Shimizu caught the same stillness at 12th Street Station, where bus driver Coen Cartier described pulling to the curb in the early fog and watching riders linger rather than board, as if the city were pausing before committing to its own momentum. Station worker Eleanor Rivera told Shimizu that fog, holidays, big votes, big games — they all alter the human flow in ways that can't be reduced to a single cause. What I find worth sitting with is that both Cartier and Rivera are essentially describing the same thing Jailon described at the lake: the way external conditions force people to slow down, look harder, and read what's actually in front of them rather than what they expect to find. A bus driver, a monitor, a station worker — none of them in the same story, but all narrating the same week.

The fog week, the illness in Chinatown, the playoff electricity: a city under pressure needs places that simply stay open without requiring anything.

At a Uptown apartment window, Teri Mitchell watches the same fog pool between buildings. Recovered from a winter illness but still moving carefully, she notes how the moisture softens edges—mailboxes, fire escapes, the quick pace Oakland usually demands. "You notice things you might otherwise rush past," she says, tracing a finger along the damp glass. Melton Neilon sees it too in the bakery's morning regulars, their coffees cupped close. "This fog’s got everyone moving slower," he observes, watching a customer linger over the steam rising from their mug. Three cycles of rain gave way to this still pause, the air heavy with bay salt and suspended decisions.
